{{Short description|Rapid spread of accurate and inaccurate information}}
{{for-multi|COVID-19 related usage of the word|Misinformation related to the COVID-19 pandemic|the adjective|Infodemiology}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2020}}

An '''infodemic''' is a rapid and far-reaching spread of both accurate and inaccurate information about certain issues.<ref name= "WHO_20200202">{{cite news |title=Novel Coronavirus(2019-nCoV) Situation Report - 13 |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20200202-sitrep-13-ncov-v3.pdf |access-date=30 July 2022 |agency=World Health Organization |date=2 February 2020}}</ref><ref name="Mooney_Juhász_202007">{{cite journal |last1=Mooney |first1=Peter |last2=Juhász |first2=Levente |date=July 2020 |title=Mapping COVID-19: How web-based maps contribute to the infodemic |journal=[[Dialogues in Human Geography]] |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=265–270 |doi=10.1177/2043820620934926 |s2cid=220415906 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zielinski |first1=Chris |title=Infodemics and infodemiology: a short history, a long future |journal=[[Revista Panamericana de Salud Pública]] |date=2021 |volume=45 |article-number=e40 |doi=10.26633/RPSP.2021.40 |pmid=33995517 |doi-access=free |pmc=8110882}}</ref> The word is a [[portmanteau]] of ''[[information]]'' and ''[[epidemic]]'' and is used as a metaphor to describe how [[misinformation]] and [[disinformation]] can spread like a virus from person to person and affect people like a disease.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Blum |first1=Dinur |last2=Smith |first2=Stacy L. |last3=Sanford |first3=Adam G.  |title=The Blackwell Encyclopedia of Sociology |chapter=Infodemics |date=2025 |pages=1–3 |doi=10.1002/9781405165518.wbeos2020 |isbn=978-1-4051-6551-8}}</ref> This term, originally coined in 2003 by [[David Rothkopf]], rose to prominence in 2020 during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name=":0" /> 

==History==
In his 11 May 2003 article in ''[[The Washington Post]]''{{emdash}}also published in ''[[Newsday]]'', ''[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]]'' of New Jersey, the ''[[Oakland Tribune]]'', and the ''[[China Daily]]''{{emdash}}foreign policy expert [[David Rothkopf]], referred to the information epidemic{{emdash}}or "infodemic", in the context of the [[2002–2004 SARS outbreak]].<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511">{{Cite news |last=Rothkopf |first=David J. |date=11 May 2003 |title=When the Buzz Bites Back |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/opinions/2003/05/11/when-the-buzz-bites-back/bc8cd84f-cab6-4648-bf58-0277261af6cd/ |access-date=19 September 2022 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |location=Washington, D.C. |page=B.01}}</ref><ref name="Rothkopf_20030514">{{cite news |last1=Rothkopf |first1=David J. |date=14 May 2003 |title=SARS Also Spurs an 'Information Epidemic' |work=[[Newsday]] |location=Long Island, N.Y. |page=A29 |id={{ProQuest|279705520}}}}</ref><ref name="Rothkopf_20030518">{{cite news |last1=Rothkopf |first1=David J. |date=18 May 2003 |title=SARS, fear, rumors feed unprecedented 'infodemic' |work=[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]] |location=Bergen County, N.J. |page=O01 |id={{ProQuest|279705520}}}}</ref><ref name="Rothkopf_China Daily_20030522">{{cite news |date=18 May 2003 |title=SARS triggers an information epidemic |work=[[Oakland Tribune]] |location=Oakland, Calif. |id={{ProQuest|351861262}}}}</ref><ref name="Ricchiardi_200306">{{cite journal |last1=Ricchiardi |first1=Sherry |date=1 June 2003 |title=On the SARS beat |journal=[[American Journalism Review]] |volume=25 |issue=5 |pages=36–42 |id={{Gale|A102904047}} {{ProQuest|216859150}}}}</ref> The outbreak of [[SARS]], which was caused by [[severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 1]] began in a remote region in [[Guangdong, China]], in November 2002. By the time the outbreak ended in May 2003, it had reached 30 countries and there were over 8,000 confirmed cases and 774 deaths.

Rothkopf, who was at that time, a member of the advisory committee's board of directors at the [[Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health]]'s [[Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security]] which provides policy recommendations to the [[United States government]] and the [[World Health Organization]],<ref name="open_phil">{{cite web |date=13 January 2017 |title=Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security — Biosecurity, Global Health Security, and Global Catastrophic Risks |url=http://www.openphilanthropy.org/focus/global-catastrophic-risks/biosecurity/center-health-security-biosecurity-global-health-security-and-global-catastrophic |access-date=February 8, 2017 |publisher=[[Open Philanthropy Project]]}}</ref> said that the infodemic was the second of two concurrent epidemics.<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511"/> Rothkopf described how the "information epidemic" transformed SARS from a regional health crisis into a "debacle" that spread globally with both economic and social repercussions.<ref name="Rothkopf_20030518"/> He said this infodemic "was not the rapid spread of simple news via the media, nor is it simply the rumor mill on steroids. Rather, as with SARS, it is a complex phenomenon caused by the interaction of [[mainstream media]], [[Alternative media|specialist media]] and [[Website|internet sites]], and 'informal' media, which is to say [[Cell phone|wireless phones]], [[text messaging]], [[pagers]], [[fax]]es, and [[e-mail]], all transmitting some combination of fact, [[rumor]], interpretation, and [[propaganda]]."<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511"/> Rothkopf citing the [[United States Department of State|State Department]], said that 2002 was the "year of the most heightened state of terrorism panic in our history" even though terrorism globally had decreased to its "lowest level since 1969".<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511"/> His company, the Washington DC–based strategic intelligence and analysis firm [[Intellibridge]], which he had founded in 1999, tracked the January 2003 Chinese reports on the outbreak. On 9 February 2003, Intellibridge provided their analysis to the U.S. defense community, and then posted the information on [[ProMED-mail]], a [[Federation of American Scientists]] website.<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511"/>

The general public did not learn of the outbreak until 23 February 2003, when an elderly woman died of SARS in her home in [[Toronto]], Canada, from Hong Kong. Her son, who spread the disease in a Toronto hospital, also died.<ref name="Low_20200224">{{cite book |last=Low |first=Donald |author-link=Donald Low |chapter=SARS: Lessons from Toronto |pages=63–71 |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK92467/ |title=Learning from SARS: Preparing for the Next Disease Outbreak: Workshop Summary |date=2004 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-09154-1 |doi=10.17226/10915 |pmid=22553895 }}</ref> With the first death in North America, the [[Western media]] began to cover the outbreak. Rothkopf said that if more had been done earlier to manage the disease as well as information about SARS, perhaps there might not have been a worldwide panic. The infodemic spread globally, far beyond the countries that had SARS victims and "set off a chain reaction of economic and social consequences".<ref name="WaPo_Rothkopf_20030511"/> It also made it harder for health organizations to control the SARS epidemic as panic spread online.<ref name="Ricchiardi_200306"/>

In his 15 December 2002 article entitled "Infodemiology: The epidemiology of (mis)information" in ''[[The American Journal of Medicine]]'',<ref name="Eysenbach_20021215">{{cite journal |last1=Eysenbach |first1=Gunther |title=Infodemiology: the epidemiology of (mis)information |journal=The American Journal of Medicine |date=December 2002 |volume=113 |issue=9 |pages=763–765 |doi=10.1016/s0002-9343(02)01473-0 |pmid=12517369 |citeseerx=10.1.1.8.8283 |s2cid=35788388 }}</ref> health researcher [[Gunther Eysenbach]] coined the term ''infodemiologist''<ref name="Eysenbach_20200629">{{cite journal |last1=Eysenbach |first1=Gunther |date=29 June 2020 |title=How to Fight an Infodemic: The Four Pillars of Infodemic Management |journal=[[Journal of Medical Internet Research]] |volume=22 |issue=6 |article-number=e21820 |doi=10.2196/21820 |pmc=7332253 |pmid=32589589 |s2cid=220120867 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and later used the term to refer to attempts at digital disease detection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eysenbach |first1=Gunther |title=Infodemiology: tracking flu-related searches on the web for syndromic surveillance |journal=AMIA Annual Symposium Proceedings |date=2006 |volume=2006 |pages=244–248 |pmid=17238340 |pmc=1839505 }}</ref><ref name="Eysenbach_20200629"/>

Use of the term ''infodemic'' increased rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic. A study found that from 2010-2020 there were 61 articles mentioning the word ''infodemic'', while between 2020 and 2021 there were 14,301 published stories using the term.<ref name=":0" /> The [[United Nations]] and the [[World Health Organization]] began using the term ''infodemic'' during the COVID-19 pandemic as early as 2 February 2020.<ref name= "WHO_20200202"/><ref>{{Cite web |date=31 March 2020 |title=UN tackles 'infodemic' of misinformation |url=https://www.un.org/en/un-coronavirus-communications-team/un-tackling-%E2%80%98infodemic%E2%80%99-misinformation-and-cybercrime-covid-19 |website=[[United Nations]]}}</ref> The related term '''''disinfodemic''''' (referring to COVID-19 [[disinformation]] campaigns) has been used by [[UNESCO]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Capaldo |first1=Giuliana Ziccardi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JJv5DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA341 |title=The Global Community Yearbook of International Law and Jurisprudence 2019 |date=October 2020 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-751355-2 |page=341 |language=en |access-date=20 May 2021}}</ref> By the time that the ''[[Journal of Medical Internet Research]]'' published their June 2020 issue featuring the WHO's framework for managing [[misinformation related to the COVID-19 pandemic|the infodemic related to the COVID-19 pandemic]], the WHO and public health agencies had acknowledged [[infodemiology]] as an "emerging scientific field" that was of critical importance during a pandemic.<ref name="Eysenbach_20200629"/> By 2021, the WHO had published a number of resources clarifying the infodemic.<ref name="WHO_INfodemic_20210226">{{cite web |date=26 February 2021 |title=Infodemic |url=https://www.who.int/health-topics/infodemic#tab=tab_1 |access-date=19 September 2022 |work=[[World Health Organization]] |quote=An infodemic is too much information including false or misleading information in digital and physical environments during a disease outbreak. It causes confusion and risk-taking behaviours that can harm health.}}</ref> At the [https://www.who.int/news-room/events/detail/2021/05/04/default-calendar/4th-virtual-who-infodemic-management-conference-advances-in-social-listening-for-public-health Fourth WHO Global Infodemic Management Conference] in 2023, the [[World Health Organization]] demonstrated large-scale taxonomic segmentation of health-related social media discourse using [[Pulsar (social listening platform)|Pulsar]], categorising posts into conceptual segments covering causes, illness narratives, treatments, and public health interventions, to provide early warnings of emerging health risks and misinformation including vaccine hesitancy across multiple countries.<ref>{{cite report |author=World Health Organization |title=WHO Fourth Global Infodemic Management Conference: Advances in Social Listening for Public Health, May 2021 |year=2023 |publisher=World Health Organization |location=Geneva |isbn=978-92-4-008103-1 |url=https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/647d61d3-8dd0-42f4-bdfb-983a45e20a60/content}}</ref>

A [[Royal Society]] and [[British Academy]] joint report published in October 2020 said of infodemics that: "[[COVID-19 vaccine]] deployment faces an infodemic with misinformation often filling the knowledge void, characterised by: (1) distrust of science and selective use of expert authority, (2) distrust in [[Pharmaceutical industry|pharmaceutical companies]] and government, (3) straightforward explanations, (4) use of emotion; and, (5) [[echo chamber]]s," and to combat the ill and "inoculate the public" endorsed Singapore's [[Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019]], which criminalises misinformation.<ref name="rsba">{{cite report |url=https://royalsociety.org/-/media/policy/projects/set-c/set-c-vaccine-deployment.pdf?la=en-GB&hash=43073E5429C87FD2674201CA19280A8E |title=COVID-19 vaccine deployment: Behaviour, ethics, misinformation and policy strategies |last1=Royal Society |last2=The British Academy |date=21 October 2020 |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |author1-link=Royal Society |author2-link=The British Academy }}</ref><ref name="sksav">{{cite news |last1=Knapton |first1=Sarah |date=10 November 2020 |title=Spreading anti-vaxx myths 'should be made a criminal offence' |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11/10/spreading-anti-vaxx-myths-should-made-criminal-offence/ |work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]] |publisher=}}</ref> The [[Aspen Institute]] even started their misinformation project before the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WRX1GRSxk-M |title=INFODEMIC – Documentary Series Launch Event |date=29 April 2021 |type=Video |publisher=[[The Aspen Institute]] |access-date=30 April 2021 |via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>

A blue-ribbon working group on infodemics, from the [[Forum on Information and Democracy]], produced a report in November 2020, highlighting 250 recommendations to protect [[democracies]], [[human rights]], and health.<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 November 2020 |title=250 recommendations on how to stop 'infodemics' |url=https://informationdemocracy.org/2020/11/12/250-recommendations-on-how-to-stop-infodemics/ |access-date=15 November 2020 |website=[[Forum on Information & Democracy]]}}</ref>

[[Merriam-Webster]] tracked its renewed usage during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=13 May 2020 |title=Infodemic: An Epidemic of Information |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/words-were-watching-infodemic-meaning |website=[[Merriam-Webster]]}}</ref>

==Definitions==
In his 11 May 2003 article in ''The Washington Post'', Rothkopf wrote that the information epidemic or "infodemic" was a "combination of "[a] few facts, mixed with [[fear]], speculation, and rumor, amplified and relayed swiftly worldwide by modern [[information technologies]]."<ref name="Rothkopf_20030518"/>

On 2 February 2020, the World Health Organization defined ''infodemic'' as a "an over-abundance of information{{emdash}}some accurate and some not{{emdash}}that makes it hard for people to find trustworthy sources and reliable guidance when they need it."<ref name= "WHO_20200202"/> A 21 February 2021 WHO publication, said that "[a]n infodemic is too much information including false or misleading information in digital and physical environments during a disease outbreak."<ref name="WHO_INfodemic_20210226"/>

Eysenbach described ''infodemiology'' as the study of "the determinants and distribution of health information and misinformation".<ref name="Eysenbach_20021215"/>

==Research during COVID-19==
As COVID-19 swept across the globe, information about how to stay safe and how to identify symptoms became vital. However, especially in the first phases of the pandemic, the amount of false, not validated and partially true information on the media was huge. Even seemingly reliable government sources did not always follow best practices in disseminating data about COVID-19, with many potentially misleading maps published on official websites.<ref name="Mooney_Juhász_202007"/><ref name="Adams1">{{cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=Aaron M. |last2=Chen |first2=Xiang |last3=Li |first3=Weidong |last4=Chuanrong |first4=Zhang |date=27 July 2023 |title=Normalizing the pandemic: exploring the cartographic issues in state government COVID-19 dashboards |journal=[[Journal of Maps]] |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=1–9 |bibcode=2023JMaps..19Q...1A |doi=10.1080/17445647.2023.2235385 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Adams2025">{{cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=Aaron M. |last2=Gallaher |first2=Adam |last3=Benitez Ou |first3=Ashley |last4=Chen |first4=Xiang |last5=Li |first5=Weidong |last6=Zhang |first6=Chuanrong |last7=Mrozinski |first7=Richard |last8=Ghosh |first8=Debarchana |title=Mapping COVID-19: Applying Ethical Strategies in Web Mapping Decisions |journal=Cartographic Perspectives |date=2025 |volume=105 |pages=67–75 |doi=10.14714/CP105.1971 |url=https://cartographicperspectives.org/index.php/journal/article/view/1971/2423 |access-date=12 April 2025|doi-access=free }}</ref> The inappropriate use of maps on these websites may have contributed to [[political polarization]] in response to COVID-19 epidemiological control measures.<ref name="Engel2022">{{cite journal |last1=Engel |first1=Claudia |last2=Rodden |first2=Jonathan |last3=Tabellini |first3=Marco |date=18 March 2022 |title=Policies to influence perceptions about COVID-19 risk: The case of maps |journal=[[Science Advances]] |volume=8 |issue=11 |article-number=eabm5106 |bibcode=2022SciA....8M5106E |doi=10.1126/sciadv.abm5106 |pmc=8932671 |pmid=35302842}}</ref> There was also a proliferation of systematic reviews of COVID-19-related evidence, not all of which was robustly conducted.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Rebecca |last2=Bethel |first2=Alison |last3=Rogers |first3=Morwenna |last4=Whear |first4=Rebecca |last5=Orr |first5=Noreen |last6=Shaw |first6=Liz |last7=Stein |first7=Ken |last8=Thompson Coon |first8=Jo |title=Characteristics, quality and volume of the first 5 months of the COVID-19 evidence synthesis infodemic: a meta-research study |journal=BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine |date=3 June 2021 |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=bmjebm–2021–111710 |doi=10.1136/bmjebm-2021-111710|pmid=34083212 |pmc=9132873 }}</ref> Researchers have pointed out a few primary challenges of communicating with the public about COVID-19. First, [[social media]] platforms that prioritize engagement over accuracy and allow fringe opinions to thrive without correction create an [[information ecology]] that is difficult to understand.<ref name="Adams2025" /> Second, as fast-moving science and politics intertwine during the pandemic, making decisions related to combatting misinformation becomes complicated by a volatile political environment and frequently changing scientific information.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Scheufele |first1=Dietram A. |last2=Krause |first2=Nicole M. |last3=Freiling |first3=Isabelle |date=December 2021 |title=Misinformed about the 'infodemic?' Science's ongoing struggle with misinformation |journal=[[Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition]] |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=522–526 |doi=10.1016/j.jarmac.2021.10.009 |issn=2211-369X |doi-access=free}}</ref> A U.S.-based survey research revealed that during March and April 2020 higher news consumption about COVID-19, especially through social media, was associated with lower levels of knowledge and more [[fake news]] beliefs.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Gerosa, T. |author2=Gui, M. |author3=Hargittai, E. |author4=& Nguyen, M. H. |year=2021 |title=(Mis) informed During COVID-19: How Education Level and Information Sources Contribute to Knowledge Gaps |journal=International Journal of Communication |volume=15 |page=22 |url=https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/view/16438}}</ref> However, preliminary research published in fall 2021 suggested that visual information (e.g., [[infographics]]) about science and scientists, designed to address trust, might be able to mitigate belief in misinformation about COVID-19.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agley |first1=Jon |last2=Xiao |first2=Yunyu |last3=Thompson |first3=Esi E |last4=Chen |first4=Xiwei |last5=Golzarri-Arroyo |first5=Lilian |date=14 October 2021 |title=Intervening on Trust in Science to Reduce Belief in COVID-19 Misinformation and Increase COVID-19 Preventive Behavioral Intentions: Randomized Controlled Trial |journal=[[Journal of Medical Internet Research]] |volume=23 |issue=10 |article-number=e32425 |doi=10.2196/32425 |pmc=8519341 |pmid=34581678 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Mitigation==
{{Essay-like|date=February 2026|section}}
Researchers have been seeking tools to combat infodemics. Gunther Eysenbach brings up four pillars of infodemic management: (1) information monitoring ([[infoveillance]]); (2) building [[Health literacy|eHealth literacy]] and [[science literacy]] capacity; (3) encouraging knowledge refinement and quality improvement processes such as [[fact-checking]] and [[Peer review|peer-review]]; and (4) accurate and timely [[knowledge translation]] which minimizes distorting factors such as political or commercial influences.<ref name="Eysenbach_20200629"/> Scholars also advocate for tech platforms to police their content more effectively, and empower individuals to make better decisions on their own to promote the emergence of truth. Social media companies may offer a variety of cues to help people make better judgments of whether a message is legitimate or not. For example, [[Facebook]] might, in addition to showing how many "likes" a post has received, allow the count of "dislikes" to offer a more symmetric view of opinions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buchanan |first1=Mark |date=September 2020 |title=Managing the infodemic |journal=[[Nature Physics]] |volume=16 |issue=9 |page=894 |bibcode=2020NatPh..16..894B |doi=10.1038/s41567-020-01039-5 |s2cid=225343682 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Research on information dissemination during the COVID-19 pandemic identified issues with standardization and presentation of related information on official U.S. government sources, specifically state and federal government COVID-19 dashboards.<ref name="Mooney_Juhász_202007" /><ref name="Adams1" /> When the most authoritative sources of information are not presenting the data accurately, bad conclusions are inevitable. The research suggested official sources for information take steps to ensure the way data are collected, analyzed, and presented is up to the highest standards and adheres to all conventions.<ref name="Adams1" /> Standards of web-maps for government agencies should be developed, widely published, and adhered to.<ref name="Mooney_Juhász_202007" /> The web-based maps and dashboards are, if properly employed, suggested as possible ways to combat infodemics in the future.<ref name="Mooney_Juhász_202007" />

However, scholars emphasize that traditionally proposed ways to combat misinformation tend to rely on the assumption that if people encounter the correct information about an issue, they will make rational decisions based on the best scientific information available.<ref name=":1" /> Research shows that this is often not the case and that people do not act in the best interest of scientific fact for reasons including "cognitive preferences for old habits, forgetfulness, small inconveniences in the moment, preferences for the path of least resistance, and motivated reasoning."<ref>{{Cite book |last=National Academies of Sciences |first=Engineering |url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/25881/encouraging-adoption-of-protective-behaviors-to-mitigate-the-spread-of-covid-19 |title=Encouraging Adoption of Protective Behaviors to Mitigate the Spread of COVID-19: Strategies for Behavior Change |date=2020-07-23 |language=en |doi=10.17226/25881|isbn=978-0-309-68101-8 |s2cid=241252994 }}</ref> Thus, combatting misinformation should rely on a more nuanced analysis of both the content of the misinformation, as well as the socio-political environment in which it was disseminated.

==Criticism==
''[[Financial Times]]'' journalist Siddharth Venkataramakrishnan said in his 20 August 2021 article that casting the spread of misinformation and disinformation in terms of disease risks oversimplifying the problem and that "unlike the status of being healthy or infected by an actual disease, what constitutes accurate information is also subject to change." Venkataramakrishnan also pointed out that the focus of the infodemic has often been on "[[Conspiracy theory|conspiracy theorists]] and [[Snake oil|snake-oil salesmen]]", largely ignoring the at times problematic actions and confusing messaging of governments and public health bodies throughout the pandemic.<ref>{{cite news |last=Venkataramakrishnan |first=Siddharth |date=25 August 2020 |title=The real fake news about Covid-19 |url=https://www.ft.com/content/e5954181-220b-4de5-886c-ef02ee432260 |url-access=subscription |work=[[Financial Times]]}}</ref>

Communication scholars Felix Simon and Chico Camargo at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]] said in their 20 July 2021 ''New Media & Society'' article that ''infodemic'' as metaphor "can be misleading, as it conflates multiple forms of social behaviour, oversimplifies a complex situation and helps constitute a phenomenon for which concrete evidence remains patchy." Pointing out that the infodemic as a concept is "journalistically powerful, intuitively satisfying, and in strong resonance with personal experiences and intuition", Simon and Camargo argue that [[empirical evidence]] for many of the claims surrounding the term is lacking. Instead of a genuine phenomenon they see the infodemic as "a territorial claim for those who want to apply their skills, a signal to others that they are working in this area, or a framing device to tie one's work to larger debates".<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Simon |first1=Felix M |last2=Camargo |first2=Chico Q |date=20 July 2021 |title=Autopsy of a metaphor: The origins, use and blind spots of the 'infodemic' |journal=[[New Media & Society]] |volume=25 |issue=8 |pages=2219–2240 |doi=10.1177/14614448211031908 |s2cid=237692119 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Along the same lines, Krause, Freiling, and Scheufele warn of difficulties related to creating "an infodemic about the infodemic" and that research surrounding the term warrants clarification and acknowledgment of uncertainties related to its novelty and impact.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krause |first1=Nicole M. |last2=Freiling |first2=Isabelle |last3=Scheufele |first3=Dietram A. |date=22 May 2022 |title=The 'Infodemic' Infodemic: Toward a More Nuanced Understanding of Truth-Claims and the Need for (Not) Combatting Misinformation |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/00027162221086263 |journal=[[The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science]] |volume=700 |issue=1 |doi=10.1177/0002716222108626 |doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 |s2cid=246965663 |access-date=21 March 2024 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
In 2023 the PC videogame ''Infodemic: Journalism in crisis'' was announced by the [[Peru]]vian [[Media literacy|media and information literacy (MIL)]] [[non-governmental organization]] [[A Mí No Me La Hacen]].<ref>{{cite web |date= |title=PODCAST_FAKE NEWS_3 |url=https://www.goethe.de/ins/pe/es/kul/sup/fake-news.html |website=[[Goethe-Institut]] |language=es}}</ref>
